 Hawaii election officials urge putting ballots in drop boxes today
 By Dan Nakaso

 Honolulu elections officials said Monday they were preparing for the possibility of long lines today at Honolulu Hale and Kapolei Hale.
 Ballots by mail were still trickling in across Oahu, while drop box traffic was higher compared to the last midterm general election in 2022. There was also a slight increase in early, in-person voting.
 The quickest way for Oahu voters to still vote in person today is to do their research at home and place ballots in a drop box outside Honolulu Hale, Kapolei Hale or at a remote drop-box location near where they live, said Rex Quidilla, administrator for Honolulu’s elections division.
 In order for their votes to be counted today, voters must return their ballots by tonight’s 7 p.m. close of voting.
 To avoid waiting in potential long lines at in-person sites at Honolulu Hale and Kapolei Hale, Quidilla said, “Do your homework before hand. That’s the easiest way.”
 For voters who place their ballots in drop box sites by tonight’s 7 p.m. end of voting, Quidilla reassured skeptics that “when you place your ballot in a drop box, the next person who handles it is a person who works for the election division.”

 Across Hawaii, voters have consistently and overwhelmingly preferred to vote early by mail since embracing mail-in voting in 2020.
 Their mail-in ballots are then delivered to county elections centers but must arrive by 7 p.m.
 As of Monday morning, however, ballots arriving across Oahu through the mail were down 27% compared to the same point in 2022.
 But ballots placed in drop boxes by Monday were up 32% compared to the same point in 2022, while early in-person voting was up 13%.
 “Overall, from the three sources, compared to the same time in 2022 we’re down 18%,” Quidilla said. “The bulk of that is in the United States Postal Service submissions.”
 The increase in early in-person voting and drop box ballots, however, were still not large enough to make up for the decline in ballots arriving by mail, Quidilla said.
 “It’s a positive at the drop boxes and the voter service centers,” he said. “It’s higher than 2022. But we fully expect long lines on the last day of voting. If you plan to come in person, as many people do, there will be lines.”
 Overall, as of Monday, 249,140 votes had been returned by voters across Hawaii — and Oahu represented the overwhelming majority of ballots cast, or 160,137, according to state elections data.
 It’s the first year that state officials are tracking statewide ballot data each day so there is no state comparison to prior elections.
 Out of all the ballots collected statewide as of Monday, 242,598 were cast by mail-in ballot. Only 5,472 were cast early and in person.
 Although small in numbers, voters who choose to vote in person on election day have delayed the release of statewide election results in both mid-term and presidential election years because any voter in line by the 7 p.m. end of voting by law must be allowed to both vote — and even register to vote.
 This year, Honolulu voters will decide between two state constitutional amendments, along with 20 county charter amendments.
 Voters who decide to vote in person today could spend as much as 45 minutes just in the voting booth because “we have such a long ballot, especially if you have to register to vote,” said Colin Moore, who teaches public policy at the University of Hawaii.
 President Donald Trump over the last few days has continued to threaten state elections officials in Democratic-controlled states like California, along with pre-emptive legal action challenging election results in Alaska even before the final votes have been cast and counted.
 On Monday, the U.S. Supreme Court, however, turned down a request by the Trump administration to require that California set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claims have been provided to noncitizens, according to media reports.
 The Supreme Court in September also opposed an effort by Trump and the head of the U.S. Postal Service to refuse delivery of mail-in ballots in states like Hawaii that refuse to turn over state voter rolls to federal officials.
 Moore believes that Trump’s campaign aimed at sowing mistrust over U.S. elections and his threats against the security of mail-in voting may be driving this year’s drop in voters sending their ballots through the mail, while drop-box and in-person voting are up.
 While Republicans, in general, and MAGA Trump supporters, in particular, remain skeptical about mail-in voting, “this election you’re kind of getting the skepticism from both sides,” Moore said.
 “President Trump has raised all of these questions about the security of mail-in ballot that discouraged Republicans from mailing in their ballots and they wanted to vote in person,” Moore said. “But now you’re getting this from liberals, as well. They’re worried that the Trump administration is going to do something that will delay the delivery from the Post Office and there could be some opportunities to interfere with elections. From some progressive groups, they’ve been told that you want to hand deliver your ballot to the drop box or vote in person. It’s not just Republicans, there are liberal Democrats who are concerned about this, too, now.”
 This year’s marquee races in Hawaii are the elections for governor and Hawaii’s two Congressional representatives.
 But Gov. Josh Green appears poised for re-­election to a second term, along with his new lieutenant governor running mate, outgoing Kauai Mayor Derek Kawakami.
 They are being challenged by lesser-known Republican candidates Gary Cordery for governor and Daniel Anthony for lieutenant governor.
 U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda faces a long-shot challenge from Republican state Sen. Brenton Awa (R, Kaneohe­-Laie-­Mokuleia).
 If Tokuda wins, she’ll return to Congress representing rural Honolulu and all of the neighbor islands. U.S. Rep. Case faces little challenge in his re-election bid to again represent urban Honolulu.
 Neither U.S. Sens. Brian Schatz nor Mazie Hirono are up for reelection.
